items.stem: How does a Raspberry Pi fundamentally differ from a typical microcontroller like an Arduino?

options.text: The Pi runs a full Linux operating system on an application processor, not bare-metal firmware
options.rationale: Correct: it is a small Linux computer, enabling services, networking and a filesystem.

options.text: The Pi has no way to control GPIO pins
options.rationale: It can control GPIO, just under an OS.
Python is a primary language on the Pi.

options.text: The Pi has less capability than an 8-bit MCU
options.rationale: It is far more capable than a typical MCU.

items.explanation: Correct: it is a small Linux computer, enabling services, networking and a filesystem.

items.stem: Why is a systemd service preferred over starting a script manually for a long-running Pi project?

options.text: It starts the script automatically at boot and can restart it on failure
options.rationale: Correct: systemd manages lifecycle and survives reboots.

options.text: It makes the Pi boot faster by skipping Linux
It converts the script to C automatically
It removes the need for networking

items.explanation: Correct: systemd manages lifecycle and survives reboots.

items.stem: Which statements about the Raspberry Pi's hardware are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Its GPIO pins operate at 3.3V, so a 5V device may need level shifting
options.rationale: Correct: driving/reading 5V directly can damage the Pi.

options.text: It has no built-in analog-to-digital converter, so analog sensors need an external ADC
options.rationale: Correct: unlike many MCUs, the Pi lacks an onboard ADC.

options.text: Its GPIO pins are 5V tolerant by default
options.rationale: False; they are 3.3V and not 5V tolerant.

options.text: It includes a built-in ADC for analog sensors
options.rationale: False; an external ADC is required.

items.explanation: Correct: driving/reading 5V directly can damage the Pi.; Correct: unlike many MCUs, the Pi lacks an onboard ADC.
